title: A catheter at midnight
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative, not targets, and no doses or order sets are given. The hospital’s credentialing decides who may insert a catheter; your unit’s protocol and the attending nephrologist come first.
intro:
You are the nephrology fellow on call at a tertiary hospital in Pasig. The hospital has granted you the privilege to insert temporary dialysis catheters, and the attending nephrologist, Dr. Cruz, is on call by phone and can come in. Mr. Joel Mercado, 34, a construction worker, has severe oliguric acute kidney injury (AKI). He is thin, with a body mass index of 20 kg/m². Dr. Cruz has decided he needs hemodialysis tonight. His potassium is being treated per protocol.

Your reference is the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2012 AKI guideline. A portable ultrasound machine is in the room; you will use it for the catheter now and for point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) tomorrow.

n1.scene: Joel is awake and oriented. His wife, Liza, steps forward: “Ako na lang po pipirma, Doc. Kami naman ang magdedesisyon.”

choices.text: Let Liza sign, since Filipino families decide together, and explain the procedure to both of them while she signs.
choices.feedback: The family may be present and help, but Joel has capacity, so Joel consents. Shared decision-making is welcome; a substituted signature is not.
choices.then: You go back to Joel. With Liza beside him, you explain the reason, the alternatives, the risks and your role in Tagalog, ask him to explain it back, and he signs.

choices.text: Joel consents with Liza present, told that you, a supervised fellow, will insert it.
choices.feedback: A capable patient consents for himself. He must know who will do the procedure and that a trainee is involved. The real risks are bleeding, arterial puncture, a collapsed lung with a neck approach, and infection. Teach-back checks what he understood. The reason, the alternatives and the risks; under ultrasound with Dr. Cruz supervising; then he explains it back in Tagalog.

choices.text: Tell them it is routine and the risk is very small, then have Joel sign quickly so dialysis is not delayed.
choices.feedback: “Maliit lang ang risk” is not informed consent. Name the real complications and your own role; this takes a few minutes and dialysis can wait that long.
choices.then: You go back to Joel. With Liza beside him, you explain the reason, the alternatives, the risks and your role in Tagalog, ask him to explain it back, and he signs.

choices.text: Say that Dr. Cruz, the consultant, will insert the catheter, because patients trust consultants more than fellows.
choices.feedback: Misstating who performs the procedure invalidates consent. Say the trainee’s role plainly, and who supervises.
choices.then: You go back to Joel. With Liza beside him, you explain the reason, the alternatives, the risks and your role in Tagalog, ask him to explain it back, and he signs.

n2.scene: A quick scan shows a patent, compressible right internal jugular vein. His groin is clean, and he has no previous lines.
n2.prompt: Which site and technique do you choose?

choices.text: Left subclavian vein by landmarks: comfortable for him, quick for you, and easy to dress.
choices.feedback: The subclavian is last for dialysis because a catheter there can narrow the vein and ruin the arm for a future fistula. Landmarks also give up the ultrasound guidance KDIGO 2012 recommends (1A).
choices.then: After the time-out, you scan again and choose the right internal jugular vein, which is patent and compressible, under real-time ultrasound.

choices.text: Femoral vein under ultrasound: no risk of a collapsed lung, and he is thin.
choices.feedback: Femoral is KDIGO’s second choice, and in Cathedia thinner patients had less femoral colonization. But his right jugular is suitable, and the groin is harder to keep clean and keeps him in bed.
choices.then: After the time-out, you scan again and choose the right internal jugular vein, which is patent and compressible, under real-time ultrasound.

choices.text: Right internal jugular vein under real-time ultrasound, tip followed all the way.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2012 puts the right internal jugular first (Not Graded) because it runs almost straight into the superior vena cava, so catheters sit and flow well. It recommends ultrasound guidance (1A); in a Cochrane review, ultrasound cut total complications by 71% and arterial puncture by 72% compared with landmarks.

choices.text: Left internal jugular vein under ultrasound, to keep the right side free for later.
choices.feedback: Left jugular is third choice. Its path bends twice, so catheters kink, flow poorly and injure the vein wall. Use it when the right is not available.
choices.then: After the time-out, you scan again and choose the right internal jugular vein, which is patent and compressible, under real-time ultrasound.

n3.scene: On your first pass the needle tip disappears from the screen. The vein still looks intact, and you think you are about at the right depth.

choices.text: Keep advancing slowly by feel; you know the depth of the vein from the scan.
choices.feedback: A needle is visible only when it lies in the ultrasound slice. Advancing without seeing the tip gives back most of the risk ultrasound removed, and the carotid artery lies right beside the vein.
choices.then: You stop, find the needle tip again in the ultrasound slice, and advance only while you can see it. The wire passes easily and the catheter goes in. Both lumens draw dark, non-pulsatile blood.

vitals.step: Catheter in; dark, non-pulsatile blood from both lumens

choices.text: Put the probe down and switch to a landmark technique, which is faster for you at this hour.
choices.feedback: That gives up the 1A recommendation for comfort. The fix is to find the needle in the slice again, not to stop looking.
choices.then: You stop, find the needle tip again in the ultrasound slice, and advance only while you can see it. The wire passes easily and the catheter goes in. Both lumens draw dark, non-pulsatile blood.

vitals.step: Catheter in; dark, non-pulsatile blood from both lumens

choices.text: Stop advancing; find the tip again; past the pass limit, call Dr. Cruz.
choices.feedback: Watching the needle during the puncture, not only marking the vein first, is what the evidence supports. An image that does not show the needle is a reason to stop, and anyone in the room may call that stop. Slide and tilt the probe and move only while you can see the tip; step back if you cannot see it within the unit’s pass limit.

vitals.step: Catheter in; dark, non-pulsatile blood from both lumens

n4.scene: The dialysis nurse is ready. “Doc, mataas pa ang potassium. Simulan na natin? The portable film takes 40 minutes.”

choices.text: Start dialysis now, since potassium is the bigger danger, and get the chest film after the session.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2012 recommends a chest radiograph promptly after a jugular catheter and before its first use (1B). A misplaced tip or a pneumothorax found after a session is found too late. Potassium treatment continues meanwhile.
choices.then: A portable chest film is taken and read before the first use: tip in a good position, no pneumothorax. Dialysis starts at 01:10, with potassium treatment continuing as ordered.

vitals.film: Read: tip in position, no pneumothorax

choices.text: Check with ultrasound that the catheter is in the vein, and start dialysis if it looks right.
choices.feedback: A good flash and a scan are reassuring, but they do not replace the film KDIGO 2012 recommends before first use. Get the film and keep treating the potassium.
choices.then: A portable chest film is taken and read before the first use: tip in a good position, no pneumothorax. Dialysis starts at 01:10, with potassium treatment continuing as ordered.

vitals.film: Read: tip in position, no pneumothorax

choices.text: A portable chest film read before the first use, with potassium treatment going on.
choices.feedback: The film confirms the tip position and excludes a pneumothorax, as KDIGO 2012 recommends (1B). The potassium is not ignored while you wait. New breathlessness or a falling oxygen saturation after a jugular attempt is a reason to call the attending at once. The nurse watches his breathing and oxygen.

vitals.film: Read: tip in position, no pneumothorax

n5.scene: Joel is still oliguric. The resident scans his lungs before the second session and finds many B-lines; the inferior vena cava (IVC) is plethoric. She asks, “Can we set today’s fluid removal to clear the B-lines?”

choices.text: Skip the ultrasound and set the goal from his weight alone, since images can mislead.
choices.feedback: Weight is essential, but you would discard a useful look at congestion. The images are not the problem; reading them alone is.
choices.then: You go back to one question, “Is he congested?”, and combine the lung and inferior vena cava images with his examination, weights and intake and output before agreeing a goal with the attending.

vitals.pocus: B-lines and IVC read with exam, weights, intake and output

choices.text: One question (“Is he congested?”), images saved and read with the exam; agree the goal.
choices.feedback: B-lines also occur in pneumonia, and IVC size changes with breathing. In the Lung Water by Ultra-Sound Guided Treatment (LUST) trial, ultrasound-guided treatment relieved congestion more often (78% versus 56%) but did not change death, myocardial infarction or heart failure. The image is a surrogate to combine with the patient. Read them with his exam, weights, intake and output and trend; agree the goal with Dr. Cruz.

vitals.pocus: B-lines and IVC read with exam, weights, intake and output

choices.text: Yes: count the B-lines and keep removing fluid until they are gone by the end of the session.
choices.feedback: A B-line count does not prescribe a fluid goal. Chasing the image risks hypotension, and improving what you see does not guarantee better outcomes.
choices.then: You go back to one question, “Is he congested?”, and combine the lung and inferior vena cava images with his examination, weights and intake and output before agreeing a goal with the attending.

vitals.pocus: B-lines and IVC read with exam, weights, intake and output

end.title: Day 5
end.text: The catheter flows well. Joel has had three sessions without a complication and is starting to pass urine. Your note records the consent, the time-out, the site and the reason for it, the ultrasound guidance, the chest film reading before first use, and the images behind each fluid decision.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A capable patient consents for himself, told the real risks and the trainee’s role, with teach-back.
  • Right internal jugular first, femoral second, left jugular third, subclavian last (KDIGO 2012, Not Graded), under ultrasound (1A).
  • Never advance a needle you cannot see. Stop, find the tip, and call if the image does not show it.
  • Chest film before first use of a jugular or subclavian catheter (1B).
  • POCUS answers one question, and its images are surrogates to combine with the patient.

See Consent and safety, Dialysis catheters and POCUS.
